mainEntity.name: How do I know my page is hacked and not just locked?

acceptedAnswer.text: Look for the hack signs: your password stops working, the email or phone on the account has changed, posts and stories appear that are not yours, or an email from Instagram says your password changed and you never asked. A plain temporary lock for suspicious activity usually lets go with the same password and one simple check.

mainEntity.name: Someone says they will bring my page back instantly for a fee. Should I trust them?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Walk away. An account only comes back through Meta’s official path, and there is no paid fast lane. These offers are scams, or people charging you to walk the same free path you can walk yourself. Your password and your money go to none of them.

mainEntity.name: Is two factor by SMS not enough?

acceptedAnswer.text: It beats having nothing by a mile. But an SMS lives on your SIM card, and a SIM card can be moved using a forged identity. An authenticator app, on your own phone, is the safer version, and it takes a few minutes more to set up.

mainEntity.name: If the page does not come back, where do I start?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start a new page with the same name and the same identity, and announce the new address everywhere else you exist: your website, your messaging channel, and the customers whose numbers you hold. And this time, from day one, keep a customer list outside Instagram as well, so one account can never again be everything you own.

Security
Your shop page got hacked? Do these things first

To your customers, that page is the shop. A hack means someone has changed the lock on your shop door. Most of the time there is a way back, as long as the first hour does not get burned on the wrong moves.
21 November 2026·9 min read·Roxana and Arshia

In this article

  1. The first hour: getting the page back, in the right order
  2. Why the email comes first: most hacks start there
  3. And if the official path does not bring it back?
  4. Prevention that actually works, not theatre
  5. The real lesson: never build it all on one password
  6. Start here, in order

Summary

  1. Spend the first hour in order: email first, then Meta’s official recovery path, then a new password and every open session closed. And trust nobody selling “instant recovery” for a fee.
  2. Most page hacks begin with the email, or with a password that ended up in someone else’s hands. Locking the page while the email stays open is not a lock at all.
  3. A page might come back, or might not. Your website and your customer list cannot be taken off you by stealing one password. Build the part of your business that is not tied to a single account.

It started, as it usually does, with messages from customers: “Has your page been hacked?” The stories were pushing cryptocurrency, the profile photo had changed, and the password no longer worked. By noon the owner had typed that password wrong three times, messaged four people promising “instant recovery”, and was about to send money to one of them.

This story is so common for Instagram shops that you could write it down like a recipe. The good news: Meta has an official path built for exactly this, and plenty of pages come back through it. The bad news: most of the real damage happens in the first hour, out of sheer panic. Trusting the wrong person. Touching things that should have been left alone.

So this article is an order of work. First, getting the page back. Then closing the door the hacker walked through. Then the prevention that keeps this day from repeating. And one honest sentence before anything else: nobody, us included, can guarantee your page comes back. Anyone who promises you that is making money out of your panic.
The first hour: getting the page back, in the right order
Do these, in exactly this order:

items: Secure the email first: if the email the page was created with is not in your hands, the page recovery is not either. From a device you trust, change the email password and close every email session you do not recognise.

Take Meta’s official path: on the Instagram login screen, tap the forgotten password option, or go straight to instagram.com/hacked. That path exists for “my account was hacked” and walks you through proving who you are, step by step.

Read Instagram’s own emails properly: if an email arrived saying the password or the account email changed, and it was not you, that same email carries a link to undo it. Only click it once you have checked who actually sent it.
Still logged in somewhere? Use it: from that device, change the password and close every other session in the account settings. Hacker out first. Then lock the door.

Tell your customers: from your personal page, or any other channel you have, say plainly that the page is not in your hands, and that no link and no card number coming from it should be trusted. The scam that follows usually runs in your name, on your own followers.

blocks.html: Why the email comes first: most hacks start there

Most shop page hacks are not magic, and nobody broke through a wall. Either the page password leaked somewhere, or someone got into the owner’s email and simply opened the door from inside with “forgot password”. So once the page is back, check these as well:

items: The email password and the page password are not the same, and neither of them gets used anywhere else.
No forwarding rule you do not know about has appeared in the email, and the recovery number on it is your own number.
The mobile number behind the page and the email is in your hands. And if your SIM lost signal for a while, for no reason, chase that up with your operator.

blocks.html: Getting the page back is half the job. Leave the door the hacker came through open, and tomorrow you will have a guest again.
And if the official path does not bring it back?
Sometimes the automatic route is not enough. What is left is this:

items: If yours is a business account, use the support path inside Meta Business Suite and the Accounts Centre. Business accounts have more ways to make contact than personal ones.
Do the identity verification with the account owner’s ID, completely and patiently. This road sometimes takes days. Sometimes weeks.
Meanwhile, stop changing the password every day and stop firing off request after request. It does not help, and it can slow the whole thing down.

blocks.html: And a serious warning, because these are exactly the days they hunt on: people will show up promising your page back through “a contact at Meta”, or by “hacking it back”, and they want money, or your password, first. They are scammers, or they are walking the same free official path and charging you for the walk. There is no paid shortcut back into an account. None.
Prevention that actually works, not theatre

items: Two factor, with an app: in the account settings, turn on two factor authentication with an authenticator app, not SMS alone. SMS beats nothing, but a SIM can be moved. The code inside an app on your own phone closes that road.
An email just for the page: one separate email, used for the shop account and nothing else, with a password that matches nothing else you own.
Keep the backup codes: print the recovery codes Meta gives you, or store them somewhere safe that is not the phone itself. On the bad day, those codes are your fastest key.

Check who is an admin, regularly: in the Accounts Centre, look at who holds access to the page and the ad account. When a colleague or an employee leaves, their access closes that day. Not a month later.

Your password goes to no service, ever: growth, scheduling and stats tools that ask for your Instagram password are opening the door to everyone. A proper service connects through Meta’s official login and never asks. And do not buy followers. A share of these hacks walk in through exactly that door.

blocks.html: That whole list takes about an hour. Our security self check asks the same kind of questions about your website and your systems, and shows you where your open places are. And if your work has grown to where its security deserves a deeper look, the penetration testing page says, honestly, what a real assessment covers and what it does not.
The real lesson: never build it all on one password

Say the worst happened anyway, and the page never came back. If your whole business was that one page, you start from zero. No customers. No record of sales. Not even a way to tell your old customers where you have gone.

Now picture the same morning for someone with their own website. Their page is hacked, and it hurts, yes. But their domain, their website and their customer list, the numbers and emails customers gave them directly, are all still standing. From there they announce the new page, and their sales do not go to sleep. In the first article of this series, Instagram page or website, we called a page rented. Security is the other half of that same sentence: what is truly yours cannot be taken from you by stealing one password.
Start here, in order

If your page was hacked today, keep the order and do not shuffle it: email, Meta’s official path, close the sessions, tell your customers. If it has not happened to you yet, spend that one hour of prevention today instead: two factor with an app, a separate email, the backup codes kept safe, and a hard look at who is an admin. And keep a second home for your business, one whose only key sits in your own hand.
Check your own locks today

The security self check asks twelve plain questions, takes a few minutes, and shows you the open places in your website and systems. For a deeper look, the penetration testing page is where we say what we cover, and what we do not.
Frequently asked questions

How do I know my page is hacked and not just locked?

Look for the hack signs: your password stops working, the email or phone on the account has changed, posts and stories appear that are not yours, or an email from Instagram says your password changed and you never asked. A plain temporary lock for suspicious activity usually lets go with the same password and one simple check.

Someone says they will bring my page back instantly for a fee. Should I trust them?

No. Walk away. An account only comes back through Meta’s official path, and there is no paid fast lane. These offers are scams, or people charging you to walk the same free path you can walk yourself. Your password and your money go to none of them.

Is two factor by SMS not enough?

It beats having nothing by a mile. But an SMS lives on your SIM card, and a SIM card can be moved using a forged identity. An authenticator app, on your own phone, is the safer version, and it takes a few minutes more to set up.

If the page does not come back, where do I start?

Start a new page with the same name and the same identity, and announce the new address everywhere else you exist: your website, your messaging channel, and the customers whose numbers you hold. And this time, from day one, keep a customer list outside Instagram as well, so one account can never again be everything you own.
